_note: The AWS worker pool: what to fill in, and the safe defaults. This file is tracked, so a clone knows what the pool needs; your own values live in the ignored `.bm/aws.json`. Same split as the voice catalogue: `voices.default.json` ships, `.bm/voices.json` is yours. No credentials belong in either file — this app runs as an IAM user created for it (docs/AWS-IAM-USER.md, and `bm-inductor aws policy` prints the policy), and `bm-inductor aws login --csv <the console's download>` stores that user's key in the ignored `.bm/aws/credentials`, 0600, in AWS's own format. There is no fallback to this machine's own AWS identity: no stored user, no AWS call. `aws show` names the user it will act as. Most of the fields below are not typed by hand: `bm-inductor aws discover` reads them off the account and writes them here, so `region` is the only field you ever type.
_note_region: Where the boxes run. A pool lives in one region: keypairs and AMIs are region-scoped, which is why `keypairs` is a map rather than a name. One of the two fields a human types — `bm-inductor aws discover --region eu-central-1`.
_note_instance_type: CPU-bound: the TTS path is a hand-written SIMD matvec and there is no GPU code, so 2 vCPU is the floor and 4 stops render queueing behind itself. **RAM decides this, and it is measured on the target platform** (`m7i-flex.large`, linux/x86_64, release build, 2026-09-20): the sidecar is **~2.85 GB resident the moment the weights are loaded** (VmHWM 2,918,708 kB) and **~2.88 GB after a dozen renders** — the load dominates and renders add ~30 MB. So **8 GiB is the size to use, and 4 GiB is not merely tight: ~2.9 GB of sidecar plus the agent and the OS will not fit in ~3.9 GB usable.** On a Free-plan account the type to pick is therefore **`m7i-flex.large`** (2 vCPU / 8 GiB, on the free-tier list). Two cautions: a macOS/arm64 build of the same binary idles at ~1.0 GB, so **measuring on the wrong platform understates this by ~2.8x**; and `models/` is 668 MB on disk, so **never size a box from `du`**. No permission this app holds can read an account's plan, so `aws show` cannot warn about that part.
_note_disk_gb: Root volume. Models 668 MB + the profile 57 MB + the segments a chapter accumulates.
_note_subnet_id: A subnet the inductor can reach. The transport is inverted — the inductor dials the box on its task port, and nothing ever dials the inductor — so a box in a genuinely private subnet with no public address and no tunnel is one that can never be driven: it sits at Offline for ever while looking healthy in the console. A default-VPC subnet maps a public address on launch, which is why the default works. `bm-inductor aws discover` fills this with that default and prints which; override it with `--subnet subnet-…`.
_note_security_group_id: Egress matters (chapter URLs, S3, the Gemini API — never the inductor, which dials the box and not the other way round); ingress must admit TWO ports from wherever the inductor runs: 22 for provisioning, and the task port (8917) for the work itself. The second is the one that gets missed, and its failure is quiet — a box with 22 open and 8917 closed launches, accepts ssh, looks healthy and is never driven. `bm-inductor aws discover` fills this with the account's *default* group and then checks both ports, because the default group has no inbound rule that admits either (a rule naming only the group is group-to-group traffic, not you). Name your own with `--security-group sg-…`: the default group is shared, so rules added to it apply to every instance using it. On a connection whose address rotates, `0.0.0.0/0` with key-only auth is the usual answer — a /32 stops matching the moment your ISP moves you (docs/AWS-IAM-USER.md step 6).
_note_iam_instance_profile: The instance profile NAME (not an ARN). Required — every launch names it, so create the role first (docs/AWS-IAM-USER.md step 4; the console creates the matching instance profile for you). `bm-inductor aws discover --instance-profile <name>` fills this; without the flag it uses the only profile in the account, and lists them rather than guessing when there is more than one. This is what lets a box pull its own asset plane from S3 instead of receiving a 668 MB upload from your connection.
_note_ssh_user: `ubuntu` on the stock Ubuntu AMIs, `ec2-user` on Amazon Linux.
_note_keypairs: region -> the EC2 keypair NAME in that region. Create the pair in the console (EC2 -> Key pairs -> Create key pair, with the console's region selector set to the same region — a keypair is invisible outside the one it was created in), then `bm-inductor aws discover --pem <the downloaded .pem>` imports it to `.bm/aws/<region>.pem` (0600) and fills the name in from the file name, checking it against the region first. Re-importing a *different* key over an existing one takes `--force`; identical bytes are left alone. `.bm/` is gitignored, so the material never enters the tree.
_note_images: region -> the AMI ID. `bm-inductor aws discover` fills this with the current Ubuntu LTS, resolved through SSM and then written here — so it is explicit and reviewable, but nobody has to hunt the AMI catalogue for it. A value already here is left alone on the next run; `discover --ami ami-…` is how you move it deliberately. It must match `ssh_user` above (`ubuntu` on Ubuntu, `ec2-user` on Amazon Linux).
_note_spot: Spot is a good fit: render and merge are both idempotent and the lease reaper requeues an interrupted task, so a reclaimed box costs a retry rather than a lost chapter.
_note_max_workers: Hard cap on concurrently registered cloud boxes. A launch that would exceed it is refused rather than left to the caller's arithmetic.
_note_ttl_hours: Default lifetime. A box that outlives its work is the whole cost of a cloud pool.
_note_tag_key: Every box this tool starts carries this tag, so `ls` and `down` can never touch anything else in the account. Its value is the profile hash the box was launched for.
